description_ru: Тихоходки, микроскопические существа, которые умеют «выключать» жизнь. Как работает криптобиоз, что на самом деле показали опыты в космосе и почему они не бессмертны.
text:
In the film of a long-forgotten decade, the hero is always indestructible, and in the film of the microscopic world, he is a plump, eight-legged creature the length of a grain of salt, ambling across a bed of damp moss with the dignified clumsiness of a bear in a snowdrift. He is the tardigrade, or water bear, and he has acquired a popular reputation for immortality that he has done almost nothing to deserve and a great deal, quietly, to earn.

The animal was first described in 1773 by a German pastor, Johann August Ephraim Goeze, who called it a "little water bear". A few years later, the Italian naturalist Lazzaro Spallanzani, who was fond of tormenting small things in the name of science, christened the group Tardigrada, meaning "slow steppers". Today more than a thousand species are known. They live in lichens, in leaf litter, in the film of water around a grain of sand, and in ocean trenches. Each has four pairs of stubby legs ending in claws, a mouth designed for piercing plant cells or other tiny animals, and a body that rarely exceeds half a millimetre. Their mouths, equipped with needle-like stylets, are used to pierce the cell walls of algae and then to drink the contents with the air of a connoisseur sampling a rather modest vintage. They are, strictly speaking, neither insects nor worms, but members of a separate phylum, distant cousins of arthropods and velvet worms.

What makes them remarkable is not their ability to endure a bad day but their ability to suspend life entirely. When the moss in which a tardigrade lives begins to dry out, the animal does not die. It retracts its legs, expels most of its water, and contracts into a shrivelled, barrel-shaped form known as a tun. In this state its metabolism falls to a tiny fraction of its normal rate, so low that it is sometimes undetectable by the instruments available. This condition is called cryptobiosis, from the Greek for "hidden life", and a tardigrade may remain in it for years. In 2016, Japanese researchers revived an individual from a sample of Antarctic moss that had been frozen for more than thirty years; the animal eventually recovered, and, to the delight of everyone concerned, laid eggs that hatched.

For decades, the explanation seemed obvious. Many organisms that survive drying, such as brine shrimp and certain nematodes, accumulate a sugar called trehalose, which replaces water around delicate molecules and turns the cell into a kind of glass. Tardigrades, however, produce comparatively little of it. In 2017 a team led by Thomas Boothby discovered that they use something stranger: a family of proteins that have no fixed shape. When the animal dries, these proteins appear to form a protective, glassy matrix inside its cells, holding the machinery of life in place until water returns. Remarkably, when the genes for these proteins were inserted into yeast, the yeast cells became considerably better at surviving desiccation. The tardigrade, in other words, has written a recipe that other organisms can follow.

Then came the question of radiation. In 2016, Japanese scientists sequenced the genome of a species called Ramazzottius varieornatus and found a protein, which they named Dsup, for "damage suppressor". When human cells in a dish were engineered to produce Dsup, they suffered markedly fewer breaks in their DNA after being exposed to X-rays. The protein seems to bind to DNA and shield it, rather like a cloak thrown over a delicate sculpture during a storm. It is a spectacular result, though one should be careful: the mechanism is still debated, and the protein has not turned anyone into a superhero.

The most famous experiment took place in 2007, when a European team sent dried tardigrades into low Earth orbit aboard the FOTON-M3 capsule. For ten days, some were exposed directly to the vacuum of space and to solar ultraviolet radiation. Upon return, those shielded from the harshest ultraviolet light revived in large numbers, and a few of those that took the full blast also recovered and, rather astonishingly, reproduced. It was the first demonstration that an animal could survive the open space environment, and it ensured the tardigrade a permanent place in the popular imagination.

That popularity, as popularity does, has bred misunderstanding. Tardigrades are not indestructible, and they are certainly not eternal. A tardigrade in its active, hydrated state is quite as vulnerable as any other small animal; it can be killed by heat, by drought arriving too suddenly, or by the unglamorous attentions of a nematode. The tun is hardy, but it cannot withstand every insult, and no tardigrade has yet been found living, say, in a volcano. Nor has anyone shown that they could survive on the surface of an exoplanet. What they have is not invincibility but a very particular and elegant set of adaptations, tuned to the ordinary hazards of life in a puddle that sometimes evaporates.

It is worth pausing on that last point, because the real story is more interesting than the myth. The tardigrade did not evolve to survive the vacuum of space; space was never one of its problems. It evolved to survive the dry summer in a patch of lichen on a rock. That its tricks happen to protect it against radiation and cold is a kind of accident, what biologists call a side effect, in the way that a coat made for a wet climate may turn out to be excellent for a blizzard. Evolution is a thrifty tinkerer, not a visionary: it rarely builds anything from scratch, and it never plans for the day after tomorrow, still less for the vacuum beyond the sky.

The practical consequences, nevertheless, are significant. Researchers are investigating whether the protective proteins could stabilise vaccines without refrigeration, preserve biological samples, or even protect astronauts and crops from radiation. These are early-stage ideas, and more than a few will fail. But the humble water bear, plodding through its moss with the unhurried confidence of a creature that has been around for more than five hundred million years, has already taught us something that no engineer could have predicted: that stillness can be a strategy, and that one of life's best defences is the willingness to wait.

questions.question: What is a tun?
questions.answer: A shrivelled, barrel-shaped dried state of the tardigrade.

questions.question: What does the protein Dsup do?
questions.answer: It protects DNA from radiation damage.

questions.question: What happened in the 2007 space experiment?
questions.answer: Tardigrades were exposed to space and some survived and reproduced.

questions.question: Why are tardigrades not truly indestructible?
questions.answer: In their active state they are vulnerable to heat, drought and predators.
